claims.title: Fence-closing strip misses whitespace variants of the closing tag
claims.text:
🟢 **P3**

**Fence-closing strip misses whitespace variants of the closing tag**

The regex only matches the exact `</untrusted_pr_text>`. Variants such as `</untrusted_pr_text >` or `< /untrusted_pr_text>` are left in place, and an LLM may still read them as closing the fence. Widening the pattern costs nothing and makes the fence harder to escape.

*Suggested fix:*

```suggestion
		safe = safe.replace(/<\s*\/\s*untrusted_pr_text\s*>/gi, "[removed]");
```

claims.title: Open-duplicate filter may also exclude the resolved finding itself
claims.text:
🟠 **P1**

**Open-duplicate filter may also exclude the resolved finding itself**

The filter drops any resolved ref when `state.findings` holds an `open` finding with the same path and title. If `state` is the prior round's state, the finding that was just resolved is still `open` there, because `resolvedThisRound` is derived from those open findings. It would then match itself and be filtered out, leaving `resolvedFindings` always empty and no thread ever auto-resolved. The new test uses two same-title findings at different lines, so it passes either way. Exclude the finding being resolved when checking for other open duplicates, for example by comparing line or id as well as path and title. Alternatively, confirm that `state` already marks resolved findings as non-open at this point, and add a positive test.

claims.title: The filter drops any resolved ref when `state.findings` contains an open finding with the same path and title. The resolved finding itself is probably one such entry, unless `state` is already updated before this point. If it is not, no ref survives and no thread is ever resolved. The only new test expects `[]`, where a second open finding at line 80 legitimately blocks the resolve, so it cannot tell the two cases apart. Please add a positive test where one resolved finding yields `resolvedFindings` with exactly that ref. It would also help to exclude the resolved finding's own entry from the check, for example by comparing the finding key.

claims.title: Production thread resolver imports from the replay module
claims.text:
🟢 **P3**

**Production thread resolver imports from the replay module**

`resolveStaleThreads` is on the webhook posting path, but it now depends on `./replay/claims.js`, which is evaluation tooling. Changes to the replay claim splitter will silently change which threads get resolved in production. Consider moving `splitInlineClaims` to a shared module, such as the ledger or a review-comment parser, and importing it from both places.

claims.title: submitted_at ordering path in the same-sha check has no test
claims.text:
🟢 **P3**

**submitted_at ordering path in the same-sha check has no test**

The new tests only cover the array-order path, where neither review has `submitted_at`. The branch where `submitted_at` overrides array order is untested, as is the mixed case where only one review has a timestamp and the comparator falls back to index order. A regression there would silently pick the wrong 'latest' review and either skip a partial review or re-run a complete one. Add a case with `submitted_at` values that contradict array order.

claims.title: submitted_at precedence over array order has no test
claims.text:
🟢 **P3**

**submitted_at precedence over array order has no test**

The new sort lets `submitted_at` override array order when both reviews have it. Both new tests omit `submitted_at`, so they only cover the index fallback. A regression in the timestamp branch (for example, reversed subtraction) would not be caught. If the API returns reviews out of order, that regression would choose the wrong review as the latest. Add a case where the array order and the timestamps disagree, for example a newer partial review listed first.

claims.title: The comparator uses `submitted_at` only when both reviews have a parseable timestamp, and otherwise falls back to array index. If some reviews have a timestamp and others don't, the ordering is not transitive, so `Array.prototype.sort` may give an implementation-dependent result for the "latest" review. In practice GitHub always sets `submitted_at` on submitted reviews, so the impact is small. Neither new test sets `submitted_at`, so the timestamp-overrides-index branch the comment describes has no coverage. Consider a test where the array order and `submitted_at` order disagree. Alternatively, sort by index only, or by timestamp only when every candidate has one.

replies.author: joeblackwaslike
replies.body: Fixed in 8a242de5: the strip now uses `/<\s*\/\s*untrusted_pr_text\s*>/gi` and still loops until stable. New tests cover `</untrusted_pr_text >`, `< /untrusted_pr_text>` and a nested fragment, and fail on the previous code.

replies.author: joeblackwaslike
replies.body: Traced first: `markResolved` sets `status = "resolved"` on the same object that stays in `state.findings`, and `resolvedThisRound` is a filter over those objects (review.ts markResolved and the resolvedThisRound assignment), so the resolved finding is not "open" at that point and its ref survives today. The check did lean on that mutation, though, and nothing tested the positive path. Fixed in dd1da94e: the duplicate check now ignores the findings being resolved by identity, and a new `buildReview` test asserts a lone resolved finding yields exactly its `{ path, title }` ref. The existing two-finding test still covers the case where a different open finding keeps the ref out.

replies.author: joeblackwaslike
replies.body: Declining for this PR. `src/ledger/github.ts:1` already imports `splitInlineClaims` from `../replay/claims.js`, so the dependency is not new here, and moving it touches the ledger and its fixtures. Tracked as a follow-up (ai-review-bot-d0u): move the splitter to a shared module and import it from both.

replies.author: joeblackwaslike
replies.body: Fixed in c05c870d by removing the comparator rather than testing it: GitHub's list-reviews API returns reviews oldest first (verified on this PR), so the latest own review at the sha is simply the last match in list order. That drops the non-transitive mixed-timestamp case entirely; the existing older-complete/newer-partial and older-partial/newer-complete tests cover the remaining behavior.
